opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think this is actually one of the most important questions, because discovering structure is really the holy grail. Learning parameters for a structure you already have is the easy part. Deep learning is very good at that. The hard part is figuring out what the right structure is in the first place.

The way TensorLogic approaches this is that a rule in logic and an equation in tensor algebra turn out to be the same thing. A logical rule is just a tensor join followed by a projection, an Einstein summation. So once you see that, structure learning in logic and architecture learning in neural networks become the same problem. That's very powerful, because you can bring together the two traditions that have been working on it, which until now have largely been separate.

In inductive logic programming, people have spent decades learning rules from data: discovering new predicates, inventing concepts that weren't in the original vocabulary. That's predicate invention, and it's basically the same thing as discovering a new representation. In deep learning, you get representation learning for free from gradient descent, but the representations are opaque, and the architecture is fixed by hand. In TensorLogic, a predicate is a tensor, and an invented predicate is just a tensor you didn't have before. Learning its contents with gradient descent is the deep learning part. Deciding that it should exist and how it relates to the others is the structure learning part. And you can do both in the same language.

There's also a really nice trick here. If you embed your objects and relations, if you work in embedding space, then you can essentially search over structures in a continuous way. You can have a soft version of the rule that gets learned by gradient descent, and then as you lower the temperature it becomes more and more like a crisp logical rule. So you get the benefits of differentiable search, but at the end you have something that's interpretable and that you can reason with soundly. That's something that neither pure deep learning nor pure symbolic AI gives you.

Now, I don't want to pretend that this solves the problem. Structure discovery is combinatorially hard, and there's no free lunch. But the language you use matters enormously, because it determines what's easy to express and therefore what's easy to search for. If your language is a bunch of matrix multiplications with nonlinearities sprinkled in, you're going to find certain kinds of structures. If your language is the set of all tensor equations, which includes all of logic programming, then the space of structures you can discover is much richer, and also much more meaningful, because it's compositional. You can learn a piece, reuse it, and combine it with other pieces. That's how science works. That's how people discover things. And I think that's what we need for AI to actually discover new knowledge rather than just interpolate the data it was trained on.

r001.rationale: It says inductive logic programming learns rules and invents predicates, but does not attribute its inefficiency to searching a very large candidate-rule space.

r002.rationale: It describes searching over structures continuously, with a soft rule learned by gradient descent and made crisper as the temperature is lowered.

r003.rationale: It explicitly equates predicate invention with discovering a new representation.

r004.rationale: It describes invented predicates as new tensors, but does not interpret objects people perceive as invented predicates.

r005.rationale: It does not connect scientific quantities such as force to predicate invention.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, this is really the crux of it, right? Because if you look at what deep learning does, it's essentially learning a very large parametric function, and the structure is fixed in advance by the architecture. And on the other side you have symbolic AI, where the structure is explicit — you have predicates, you have rules — but it's largely hand-coded, and learning it has always been the hard part. What tensor logic does is it collapses those two into a single construct. The key observation is that a logical rule and an Einstein summation are the same thing. A rule like "X is a grandparent of Z if X is a parent of Y and Y is a parent of Z" is literally a tensor equation: you take the parent tensor, you multiply it by itself, you sum out the intermediate index Y, and you get the grandparent tensor. Once you see that, the whole language is just tensor equations. Neural networks are tensor equations, logic programs are tensor equations, kernel machines, graphical models — all of them.

So now to your question. Discovering structure in the symbolic world is the problem of inductive logic programming, or structure learning in graphical models, and it's historically been a combinatorial search — you propose a clause, you test it, you refine it, and it's very expensive and very brittle. In the neural world, you don't discover structure at all; you just fit weights. In tensor logic, the structure is itself expressed as tensors, which means that search over structures and search over parameters become the same kind of operation. You can relax the discrete choice of which rule to include into a continuous one, do gradient descent, and then sharpen it back into a crisp rule. Or you can do it in the other direction — you can have a symbolic search where each candidate is immediately a differentiable program that you can evaluate end to end. And the embedding aspect matters here too, because in tensor logic the objects — the constants, the predicates — live in an embedding space, so "discovering a new concept" can mean finding a new direction, a new region in that space, and then naming it and reasoning about it symbolically. That's something neither paradigm does well on its own.

The other thing I'd say is that this gives you reasoning in embedding space with the reliability of logic. One of the things that drives me crazy about current systems is that they hallucinate, and they hallucinate precisely because there's no notion of sound inference. In tensor logic you have a temperature parameter: at zero it's pure deduction, everything that comes out is entailed by what went in, and as you raise it you get more analogical, more generalizing, but in a controlled way. So when you're discovering new representations, you're not just hoping the network stumbled onto something meaningful — you can ask what follows from it, you can check it, and you can compose it with everything else you already know. I think that's ultimately what's going to get us past the current plateau: not bigger models, but a language where learning and reasoning are the same thing.

r001.rationale: It describes traditional inductive logic programming as an expensive, brittle combinatorial search over clauses, which conveys the cost of searching candidate rules.

r002.rationale: It says discrete choices about which rules to include can be relaxed and handled with gradient descent, then sharpened back into rules.

r003.rationale: It frames discovering a new concept by finding a region or direction in embedding space, then naming it for symbolic reasoning, as representation discovery.

r004.rationale: It does not interpret objects people perceive as invented predicates.

r005.rationale: It does not connect scientific quantities such as force to predicate invention.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to treat structure itself as something you can learn, rather than something that has to be fixed before learning begins. In a neural network, we typically choose an architecture and then learn the weights. In logic, we can learn rules, but searching over possible rules is a difficult combinatorial problem. We’d like to bring those two capabilities together.

The idea with TensorLogic is that logical rules and neural computations can be expressed in a common language of tensor operations. That gives us a way to connect learning continuous representations with discovering discrete structure. A representation can make a useful relationship easier to discover, and a discovered relationship can guide the learning of a better representation.

For example, suppose you’re learning about objects and their interactions. You want to learn not just features that predict the next observation, but potentially new concepts and relations that explain many observations. Those concepts then become building blocks for further learning.

Now, a common language doesn’t by itself solve the search problem. You still need ways to propose structures, evaluate them, and control complexity. But it gives us a framework in which representation learning and structure learning can inform each other, rather than being separate stages.

r001.rationale: It describes rule search as a difficult combinatorial problem, but does not attribute inefficiency to traditional Inductive Logic Programming or clearly state that it searches a very large candidate-rule space.

r002.rationale: It says TensorLogic can connect representation learning and structure learning, but does not state that gradient descent itself performs structure learning.

r003.rationale: It discusses discovering new concepts and relations, but does not identify predicate invention as representation discovery.

r004.rationale: It gives an example involving objects and interactions, but does not interpret perceived objects as invented predicates.

r005.rationale: It does not connect scientific quantities such as force to predicate invention.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to treat structure as something you can learn, rather than something you have to specify once and for all. In a neural network, we typically fix the architecture and learn the weights. In a logic program, we typically specify the rules and then do inference. What we really want is to learn both the rules and the representations that make those rules useful.

TensorLogic gives us a way to express those things in a common language. You can have continuous, distributed representations, but you can also have variables, relations, and compositions of relations. So discovering a new structure might mean discovering a useful rule, introducing a new predicate, or learning a representation in which a complicated relationship becomes simple.

But there's an important distinction here: providing a language in which you can express those discoveries doesn't automatically give you an algorithm that makes them. You still need to search over structures, and that is a much harder problem than optimizing parameters in a fixed structure. The opportunity is to combine the two: use continuous optimization where it works well, and structural search where you need to change what the model can express. That's the direction I find exciting.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention Inductive Logic Programming or attribute its inefficiency to searching a large space of candidate rules.

r002.rationale: It says TensorLogic’s expressive language does not automatically provide a structure-learning algorithm and distinguishes continuous optimization from structural search.

r003.rationale: It explicitly describes introducing a new predicate as one way of discovering a new structure.

r004.rationale: The response does not interpret objects people perceive as invented predicates.

r005.rationale: The response does not connect scientific quantities such as force to predicate invention.
